title: Band lineup on the stand and arrival of piano
summary: He describes the old band order, bass at left through drums at the end, and the piano entering bands around 1915, when he sat in for the drummer at Rice's.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: In the old days, say in Millenburg or in the Hall, how would they line the band up? Would the drums be in one spot and the bass in another one?
No, you see, the bass was always on the left-handed side, see. And then the guitar, the clarinet, the cornet, trombone, the drums on the other end, see what I mean? Line up that way, see.
Facing the band, the bass would be on the left? Left, left, yeah. Yeah, if I'm facing the band, the bass would be on the left. Yeah. And name the other instruments again?

The bass, the banjo, the guitar, or you use the banjo. Well, most likely the old days they used the guitar, she didn't use the banjo. The banjo came in later, came back later on, you know, in years. The guitar, clarinet, the cornet, trombone, and drums on the end. That's the way they played.
And when did the piano come into the line?

Well, the piano, well, I'll tell you about the piano. When they put a piano in the band, I mean, I couldn't get what the piano. You know, so used to playing just the bass and the guitar, you know, it was so nice, you know. I wasn't used to putting custom to it, you know what I mean? And I said, oh, this don't make sense, I mean, because we never had no piano in the band, you know. Pianos always played alone by themselves, you know. I remember the district, all the guys, you know, played mostly alone, you know. Until later on in years, around about, I would say around 1915, then the band started having pianos. You know, maybe a little before that, yeah. Maybe a little before that they had pianos. Because when I worked at a district, I was working, I was about 16 years old, I used to put on Long Charles. I used to work at Rice, with a man who's pressing him. I used to go in, I don't call it, Hendrick Morton's place. I used to replace him. Hendrick Morton was working there, Hendrick Morton was working at, a few clothes, I think. And old man, Conchal, was working at Rice. That's right, I used to replace him. Because his son used to, a little little Conchal would play the clarinet now, or he used to come and engage me. He said, my daddy said, can you go in his place tonight? So, I said, okay. I had one pair of trousers, one pair of Long Charles, it was a gift to me. And I used to put them on, and go sit in his place.
Would the piano be on the right or the left, though? How would it vary?
No, the piano was facing the back of us. And the band was facing the audience. Our piano player had his back to us. That's the way that was at that time.
And who would be right directly in front of the piano player?
